rows.subtype: Approach: letting go of a small item after a fair search [Revision]
rows.description: After searching properly and asking, a girl still cannot find her cheap sharpener. She decides it is not worth more time, borrows one and adds her name to the next one.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, emotion-aware planning, externalising on paper
this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6

rows.subtype: Approach: listing every task and estimating time [Thinking]
rows.description: A Class 5 child lists maths sums, a Hindi paragraph and a drawing, then guesses ten, twenty and thirty minutes each. Seeing the total is one hour helps her feel the work is finite and not scary.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: externalising on paper, impulsive action, time-boxing

rows.subtype: Approach: doing the hardest subject first while fresh [Action]
rows.description: A boy starts with maths word problems right after his snack because his head is clear. He saves colouring the map for last, when he is tired and the task is easy.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: externalising on paper, impulsive action, time-boxing

rows.subtype: Approach: doing the easy fun parts first [Pitfall]
rows.description: A girl finishes the drawing and copying work first because they feel nice. By 8 pm only the hard sums remain, she is sleepy, and she rushes them with mistakes.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: externalising on paper, time-boxing

rows.subtype: Approach: pushing it off until just before bedtime [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child tells himself there is plenty of time and plays cricket and watches cartoons. At 9 pm he realises the science diagram takes an hour, and he starts crying and asking a parent to help.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: impulsive action, time-boxing

rows.subtype: Approach: seeing the crowded evening and redoing the plan [Revision]
rows.description: Halfway through, a boy notices a cousin is visiting at 6 pm. He moves the sums to before dinner, and does the reading after the guests leave, so nothing is left undone.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: externalising on paper, impulsive action, time-boxing

rows.subtype: Approach: working in short blocks with small breaks [Action]
rows.description: A child sets a kitchen timer for twenty minutes of work and then five minutes of water and stretching. The breaks make the next block easier and the whole thing gets done before dinner.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: externalising on paper, impulsive action

rows.subtype: Approach: working next to a sibling doing their own homework [Action]
rows.description: A girl sits at the same table as her older brother, who is studying. Seeing him work quietly makes it easier to keep going, and she asks a question only when truly stuck.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: externalising on paper, impulsive action, time-boxing

rows.subtype: Approach: asking for help the moment a problem is stuck [Revision]
rows.description: A child gets stuck on a fractions question for fifteen minutes, then notices he is only getting upset. He puts a star next to it, asks his mother, and gets on with the other questions.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: externalising on paper, impulsive action, time-boxing

rows.subtype: Approach: rushing to finish and skipping the checking [Pitfall]
rows.description: A boy wants to go out to play so he scribbles answers fast and closes the notebook. Next day the teacher marks two sums wrong for copying errors he would have caught in a minute of checking.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: externalising on paper, time-boxing
